title: Dust and worlds (section 30)
hookLine: a world ground into dust: are the specks many? the world is not a world, so called

cards: Late afternoon, and the light comes sideways through a kitchen window. Suddenly the air, which looked empty, is full. Specks drift, turn, flare and vanish.

They were there the whole time; the light just caught them. A child on a beach makes the same discovery in reverse. She builds a castle, proud of every tower, and an hour later the tide makes it sand again.
Which one was it really? Section thirty of the Diamond Sutra blows that question up to the size of a world.

teach.b: The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: suppose someone ground a whole vast world system down to dust, finer and finer. Would that heap of specks be many? Many indeed, Subhuti says.
Then his reason, and it's a strange one. If the heap were a real thing in itself, the Buddha would not have called it a heap.

teach.h: A HEAP IS CALLED A HEAP.
teach.b: What's taught as a heap of specks is taught as no heap, and that's why it's called a heap of specks. He turns the same blade on the world.
The world system the Tathagata speaks of is not a world system; that's why it's called a world. Why say this?
Because if a world really existed as one solid thing, Subhuti says, that would be a grasping at a lump: taking a heap of parts as one fixed whole.
The Buddha answers that this grasping at a lump can't truly be put into words. It isn't a thing. Yet ordinary people get hold of it anyway.
The mind is a lump-maker. My whole life. This entire mess.
Everything is falling apart. Each feels like one solid block. Section thirty grinds the block gently into specks, and then won't let you make the specks into solid little blocks either.
Neither the world nor the dust is the final, fixed thing. What's left is closer to that kitchen air: full, moving, and lit.

how: Students of the Diamond Sutra in Mahayana communities read section 30 as a lesson in how the mind makes solid wholes out of parts; it's chanted with the rest of the sutra and taken up in study and meditation.

o: a world ground to specks, and neither one a fixed thing
a story of how the universe was made from specks
the belief that the world is an illusion made of dust

games.q: a world of dust: tap the pairs.
p: no heap, so called a heap
no world, so called a world
taking parts as one fixed whole

s: Subhuti says the specks would be few
he says many indeed, and then says the heap is only called a heap.
the sutra calls the world itself 'so called'
the world system is not a world system; that's why it's called a world.
the dust is the final real thing under the world
the heap of specks is no heap too; neither whole nor parts is fixed.

games.q: you're Subhuti. a whole world has been ground into dust. the Buddha asks: are the specks many?
o: few: a world is not so big
many: yet a heap is only called a heap
no answer: they can't be counted
games.why: many indeed, he says; but if the heap were a real thing, the Buddha wouldn't call it a heap. so it's called a heap of specks.

practice: If there's a window with sun nearby, find the angle where the air shows its specks and watch them drift; if not, close your eyes and let the mind's own pictures drift the same way.
Hold one thing that feels like a solid lump today, a worry, a task, a judgment of yourself. See it as specks, a few moments, thoughts and sensations moving in the light, and let it stay loose.

wordCard.voice: Dust and worlds. Section thirty: a world ground into dust; the heap of specks is no heap, and the world no world, and so they're called heap and world. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a world system; the 'world' that section 30 grinds into dust and calls a world, so called.

carryVoice: Your line: a world of dust. A heap is only called a heap. I'll be here tomorrow.
